notes.definition: The test for chlorine uses damp litmus paper. When damp litmus paper is put into chlorine gas, the litmus paper is bleached and turns white.
explanation: To test a gas for chlorine, hold a piece of damp litmus paper in the gas, for example at the mouth of a test tube or near an electrode where gas is forming. If the gas is chlorine, the litmus paper is bleached and turns white. Blue litmus paper may turn red briefly before it is bleached, because chlorine forms an acidic solution with water, but the key result is that the colour is removed and the paper turns white.

The litmus paper must be damp. Chlorine dissolves in the water on the paper and forms substances that act as bleach. Dry litmus paper is not bleached quickly, so a dry paper could give a false negative result. The same bleaching action is why chlorine compounds are used in household bleach and to kill microorganisms in drinking water and swimming pools.

Chlorine is a green-yellow (pale green) gas with a sharp, choking smell. It is toxic, so tests should be done in a fume cupboard or with very small volumes, and you should never smell it directly. Its colour can be a useful clue, but colour alone is not a reliable test, because at low concentration chlorine looks almost colourless.

In the laboratory, chlorine is most often met in electrolysis. When concentrated sodium chloride solution (brine) is electrolysed, chlorine is produced at the positive electrode (anode), hydrogen at the negative electrode and sodium hydroxide solution is left. Chlorine is also produced at the anode when molten sodium chloride or other aqueous chloride solutions such as copper chloride solution are electrolysed. In each case chloride ions lose electrons at the anode: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻.
keyFacts: Test: put damp litmus paper into the gas.
Positive result: litmus paper is bleached and turns white.
Blue litmus may turn red first, then white.
The litmus paper must be damp, because chlorine must dissolve in water to bleach it.
Chlorine is a toxic green-yellow gas; use a fume cupboard.
Chlorine forms at the anode when chloride solutions or molten chlorides are electrolysed.
Electrolysis of brine gives chlorine (anode), hydrogen (cathode) and sodium hydroxide solution.
Chlorine's bleaching and disinfecting properties are used in bleach and water treatment.

Having had its colour removed; in the chlorine test, the litmus turns white.
Slightly wet with water, so that a gas can dissolve on the surface.
Concentrated sodium chloride solution; its electrolysis produces chlorine, hydrogen and sodium hydroxide.

equations.name: Electrolysis of brine (overall)
equations.formula: sodium chloride + water → hydrogen + chlorine + sodium hydroxide

workedExamples.title: Identifying the gas at the anode
workedExamples.question: Concentrated sodium chloride solution is electrolysed. A pale green gas forms at the positive electrode. Name the gas and describe a test to confirm it.
steps: In electrolysis of a chloride solution, chloride ions are attracted to the anode (positive electrode).
They lose electrons and form chlorine gas, which is pale green.
Hold damp litmus paper near the anode or in a tube of the gas.
workedExamples.answer: Chlorine; damp litmus paper is bleached and turns white.

workedExamples.title: Predicting the observation with blue litmus
workedExamples.question: A student holds damp blue litmus paper in chlorine. Describe what the student sees.
steps: Chlorine dissolves in the water on the paper, forming an acidic solution.
The blue litmus may turn red first.
The bleaching action then removes the colour.
workedExamples.answer: The paper may turn red briefly, then is bleached white.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often write that chlorine 'turns litmus red' as the test.
misconceptions.right: In fact the positive result is that damp litmus is bleached white. Many acidic gases turn blue litmus red, so red alone does not identify chlorine.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often forget that the litmus paper must be damp.
misconceptions.right: In fact chlorine must dissolve in water to bleach the paper. Dry litmus may show no change.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think chlorine is produced at the cathode in electrolysis.
misconceptions.right: In fact negative chloride ions are attracted to the positive anode, where they lose electrons to form chlorine.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often use the gas's colour or smell to identify chlorine.
misconceptions.right: In fact chlorine is toxic and should not be smelled, and its colour is faint at low concentration; use the damp litmus test.

realWorld: Chlorine is added to drinking water and swimming pools to kill harmful microorganisms.
Household bleach contains sodium chlorate(I), made by reacting chlorine with sodium hydroxide, both products of brine electrolysis.
The chlor-alkali industry electrolyses brine to make chlorine for PVC plastic, disinfectants and medicines.
higherTier: At the anode, chloride ions are oxidised (lose electrons): 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻.
examTips: Always say 'damp litmus paper' and 'bleached' or 'turns white'. Both words matter for the marks.
If blue litmus is used, you may mention it turns red first, but the mark is for it being bleached.
In electrolysis questions, chlorine forms at the anode whenever chloride ions are present in a concentrated solution or molten compound.
Mention a fume cupboard if asked about safety, because chlorine is toxic.
summary: Test: damp litmus paper in the gas.
Chlorine is toxic and green-yellow; use a fume cupboard.
Chlorine forms at the anode when chlorides are electrolysed.

questions.question: What is used to test for chlorine?
markScheme: 1 mark: Damp litmus paper
questions.explanation: Damp litmus paper is used. Limewater tests for carbon dioxide, a glowing splint for oxygen and a burning splint for hydrogen.

questions.question: What is the positive result of the test for chlorine?
options: The litmus is bleached and turns white
markScheme: 1 mark: The litmus is bleached and turns white
questions.explanation: Chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper, removing its colour.

questions.question: What colour is chlorine gas?
markScheme: 1 mark: Green-yellow
questions.explanation: Chlorine is a pale green-yellow gas. Bromine vapour is brown and iodine vapour is purple.

questions.question: Why must the litmus paper be damp in the chlorine test?
options: So that it does not burn
So that it changes colour faster in air
So that the chlorine dissolves and can bleach it
markScheme: 1 mark: So that the chlorine dissolves and can bleach it
questions.explanation: Chlorine must dissolve in the water on the paper to bleach it; dry paper would not show the result clearly.

questions.question: At which electrode is chlorine produced during the electrolysis of concentrated sodium chloride solution?
markScheme: 1 mark: Anode (positive electrode)
questions.explanation: Negative chloride ions move to the positive anode and are discharged as chlorine. Hydrogen forms at the cathode.

questions.question: Which safety precaution is most important when testing for chlorine?
options: Keep the gas away from naked flames
markScheme: 1 mark: Work in a fume cupboard
questions.explanation: Chlorine is toxic, so a fume cupboard removes it safely. It is not flammable, and dry litmus would make the test unreliable.

questions.question: Which half equation shows how chlorine is formed at the anode?
markScheme: 1 mark: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻
questions.explanation: Chloride ions lose electrons (oxidation); two chlorine atoms form a Cl₂ molecule, so electrons are on the right.

questions.question: A gas turns damp blue litmus red but does not bleach it. Which conclusion is correct?
options: The gas is acidic but not chlorine
markScheme: 1 mark: The gas is acidic but not chlorine
questions.explanation: Chlorine would bleach the paper. Turning red only shows the gas forms an acidic solution, for example carbon dioxide or hydrogen chloride.

questions.question: Which of these electrolysis experiments produces chlorine at the anode?
markScheme: 1 mark: Electrolysis of copper chloride solution
questions.explanation: Chloride ions are needed. Sulfate solutions give oxygen at the anode, and lead bromide gives bromine.

questions.question: Which word describes what happens to the colour of damp litmus paper in chlorine?
markScheme: 1 mark: Bleached
questions.explanation: Chlorine bleaches the paper, removing its colour so it turns white.

questions.question: Describe the test for chlorine and give the result.
markScheme: 1 mark: put damp litmus paper into the gas
1 mark: litmus is bleached / turns white
questions.explanation: Both 'damp' and 'bleached/white' are needed for full marks.

questions.question: Name the gas produced at the positive electrode when brine is electrolysed.
markScheme: 1 mark: chlorine
questions.explanation: Chloride ions are discharged at the anode in concentrated chloride solutions.

questions.question: A student holds damp blue litmus paper in a tube of chlorine. Describe what the student sees, in order.
markScheme: 1 mark: turns red (first)
1 mark: then bleached / turns white
questions.explanation: Chlorine forms an acidic solution with water, then its bleaching action removes the colour.

questions.question: Give two reasons why chlorine is tested in a fume cupboard and not by smelling it.
markScheme: 1 mark: chlorine is toxic/poisonous
1 mark: it irritates/damages the lungs or airways if breathed in
questions.explanation: Never identify gases by smell in the lab; chlorine is especially dangerous.

questions.question: Name the three products of the electrolysis of concentrated sodium chloride solution.
markScheme: 2 marks: chlorine, hydrogen and sodium hydroxide (solution)
1 mark: any two
questions.explanation: Chlorine forms at the anode, hydrogen at the cathode, and sodium hydroxide remains in solution.

questions.question: Explain why chlorine is formed at the anode, not the cathode, when sodium chloride solution is electrolysed.
markScheme: 1 mark: chloride ions are negative so they are attracted to the positive electrode (anode)
1 mark: there they lose electrons (are oxidised) to form chlorine molecules: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻
questions.explanation: Opposite charges attract; oxidation always happens at the anode.

questions.question: Suggest why the bleaching property tested in the chlorine test makes chlorine useful in water treatment.
markScheme: 1 mark: chlorine is very reactive / the same chemicals that bleach dyes also damage cells
1 mark: so it kills bacteria/microorganisms in water
questions.explanation: The reactive substances formed when chlorine dissolves in water destroy dyes and microorganisms.

questions.question: State the colour that damp litmus paper turns in chlorine.
markScheme: 1 mark: white (bleached)
questions.explanation: Chlorine bleaches the indicator dye, so the paper turns white.

questions.question: Copper chloride solution is electrolysed. A gas forms at one electrode and a brown solid at the other. Identify the gas, state at which electrode it forms, and describe how to test for it, including a safety precaution.
markScheme: Indicative content: gas is chlorine
Forms at the anode (positive electrode)
Brown solid is copper at the cathode
Test: hold damp litmus paper near the anode
Result: litmus bleached / turns white (blue may turn red first)
Safety: fume cupboard / small scale / ventilated room because chlorine is toxic
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): gas, electrode, test and result all correct, with safety precaution
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): gas identified or test described
questions.explanation: Chloride ions are discharged at the anode, giving chlorine, which bleaches damp litmus.

questions.question: A student has four unlabelled test tubes containing hydrogen, oxygen, carbon dioxide and chlorine. Describe a sequence of tests the student could use to identify all four gases. For each test give the result, and explain why the student should test for chlorine safely.
markScheme: Indicative content: chlorine: damp litmus paper is bleached / turns white (could also note pale green colour)
Hydrogen: burning splint gives a pop
Oxygen: glowing splint relights
Carbon dioxide: bubble through/shake with limewater, turns milky
Logical order, for example litmus test first (non-destructive), then limewater, then splints
Elimination: once three are identified the fourth can be confirmed
Safety: chlorine is toxic; use a fume cupboard; do not smell gases
Hydrogen and air can explode; use small volumes
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): all four tests and results correct in a logical sequence with safety reasoning
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): three tests with correct results, or four with errors
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two correct tests
questions.explanation: Top answers give all four tests with correct results, a sensible order and specific safety points for chlorine.

questions.question: A student puts DRY blue litmus paper into chlorine. Very little change is seen. What is the best explanation?
options: Chlorine needs water on the paper to dissolve in before it can bleach it
Chlorine is less dense than air and escaped
markScheme: 1 mark: Chlorine needs water on the paper to dissolve in before it can bleach it
questions.explanation: The test requires damp paper. Chlorine bleaches both red and blue litmus, and it is denser than air.

questions.question: In the electrolysis of brine, how could you tell which electrode produces chlorine and which produces hydrogen?
options: Both gases relight a glowing splint
Damp litmus is bleached near the anode; a burning splint pops with gas from the cathode
Damp litmus is bleached near the cathode; the anode gas pops
markScheme: 1 mark: Damp litmus is bleached near the anode; a burning splint pops with gas from the cathode
questions.explanation: Chlorine (anode) bleaches damp litmus; hydrogen (cathode) burns with a pop.

questions.question: Chlorine is used to make bleach. Which property of chlorine is shown by the gas test?
markScheme: 1 mark: It is a bleaching agent
questions.explanation: The test relies on chlorine removing the colour of the litmus dye, which is its bleaching action.

questions.question: When dilute (not concentrated) sodium chloride solution is electrolysed, the gas at the anode only slowly bleaches damp litmus and also relights a glowing splint. Suggest what the gas is.
markScheme: 1 mark: a mixture of oxygen and chlorine
1 mark: bleaching shows some chlorine; relighting a glowing splint shows oxygen
questions.explanation: With dilute chloride solutions, oxygen from water is also produced at the anode, so the two tests together show a mixture.

questions.question: Explain why litmus paper that is bleached white cannot be used afterwards to test whether a solution is acidic or alkaline.
markScheme: 1 mark: the indicator dye has been destroyed/removed, so it can no longer change colour
questions.explanation: Bleaching is a permanent chemical change to the dye, which is why it is a clear positive result for chlorine.
